doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Father, Condon concerts and choosing music
summary: His jazz-loving father took him to Eddie Condon concerts; he decided on music as high school went badly; teacher tolerated jazz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did you find a point growing up that, you started to think about this as a career?

Yeah, when I started doing lousy in high school. After, maybe I was about fifteen, sixteen, I’d still been studying piano but my jazz influence came into me through my father, who loved jazz music, could have been a musician, wasn’t. Had all the instincts. And he used to take me to jazz concerts. I was just talking about that to someone earlier. The first concert I attended was at Carnegie Hall. Eddie Condon had a big, massive jazz party, right on stage there. He had four pianos, four grand pianos, four basses, maybe three or four drummers, all lined up. And of course it was small groups at first and then this was the finale with all the players. But the informality of it, I just couldn’t understand. He’s walking around the stage while the guys were playing and he’s chatting with this guy and he’s pointing to this guy to take a solo, you next he’s going. And then he’d get on the microphone and mumble something.

Well Eddie was that kind of a character. And I couldn’t quite figure this out. And at the end of the concert my dad asked me, “How did you enjoy it?” I said it was all right, just kind of confusing. I was maybe fourteen, fifteen. And he took me to another one later on, there was just one band playing. I forget where it was. The Ziegfield Theater I think. And there was a bunch of Condonites, you know.

And I caught it and they started playing and all of a sudden I got a chill. The sound of it, the brass, you know, it was so exciting to hear that raw sound coming through. And I said gee this is good. This is good. This I understood more than the other. Now I understand the other, more so now. But at the time it was kind of confusing. And I thought this might be something I might want to do. I was doing lousy in high school. My interest wasn’t there. I mean two classes I was good at — music appreciation class and phys ed, or sports, or whatever, you know, baseball and things like that I was pretty good at. But the regular curriculum, no, it wasn’t for me. And I barely graduated but my interest in music, my teacher was very instrumental in helping me. She was an ex-concert pianist, retired. And she’d give me a lesson and I’d play, I’d do the lesson, perform it for her, whatever she gave me the week before. And at the end of the lesson she’d say okay, now play something for me. And I’d play some “Sweet Lorraine,” something to that effect. And she sat back and loved it. She loved that I was doing that. A lot of teachers in those days would have resented that and said how dare you. No, she was pretty cool about that.
